I was wondering why the filter wouldn't work as expected even though the cgroup numbers are correctly inserted to the set. Looking at [here](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/23d04328444a8fa0ca060c5e532220dac8e8bc26/net/netfilter/nft_meta.c#L174), [here](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/23d04328444a8fa0ca060c5e532220dac8e8bc26/include/linux/cgroup-defs.h#L783) and [here](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/23d04328444a8fa0ca060c5e532220dac8e8bc26/include/linux/cgroup-defs.h#L764), it seems that `meta cgroup` operates with `net_cls` cgroup v1 controller.

The cgroupv2 version, `socket cgroupv2 level x "path"` has the same problems as cgroupv1 ID had, the path (/sys/fs/cgroup/path) is resolved immediately when the rules are loaded and this fails since the cgroups don't exist yet. This is exactly what https://github.com/mk-fg/systemd-cgroup-nftables-policy-manager tries to solve. The NFT set approach can't work since strings can't be used in sets.

Maybe cgroupv2 could be made to work with bit more invasive approach: PID1 would install filters which match cgroups (once they are realized). The filter would then set socket marks. Firewall rules would then be able to use the socket marks as they please.

> Hmm it seems that in more recent `nft` you can actually match on Cgroup paths directly? Wouldn't that be the way to go?

The path is resolved when the firewall rules are loaded and if the cgroup path doesn't exist (since the service hasn't been started yet), it will fail. This makes them equally useless directly.

Perhaps there's a way (PID1 would manage cgroupv2 rules which use socket marks and store the marks in sets so that rules can reference them).

Yeh sounds to me like upstreaming something along the lines of https://github.com/mk-fg/systemd-cgroup-nftables-policy-manager seems to be the way to go. Also if it turns out that `cgroup` mark only works for `net_cls` (which doesn't exist in cgroups v2)

> Yeh sounds to me like upstreaming something along the lines of https://github.com/mk-fg/systemd-cgroup-nftables-policy-manager seems to be the way to go.

It works by loading arbitrary NFT filters when a service starts. I think this level of complexity was rejected earlier, leading to simpler `IPAddressAllow=`/`IPAddressDeny=` features. Maybe this could be implemented with `ExecStartPre=+nft -f /etc/nftables-%p.conf` with no changes, if the cgroup is realized and unchanging at that point. If not, perhaps that could be ensured with a new flag (like `[+-@:!]` now). Also `ExecStartPost=+nft ...` may work, though the starting order may leave a vulnerable window depending on the firewall design.

Perhaps network namespace support could be beefed up so that interfaces would be available inside the namespace without `ExecStartPre=` stuff.

> Also if it turns out that `cgroup` mark only works for `net_cls` (which doesn't exist in cgroups v2)

This is indeed the case.
Updated with `DynamicUserNFTSets=` directive for automatic insertion of UID of the dynamic user into NFT set.

In this version: `Network.IPv4NFTSet=nfproto:table:set` and `Network.IPv6NFTSet=nfproto:table:set`.

I noticed a possible problem in testing this that if the set already includes a range (10.0.0.0/8) and `networkd` changes the address (say, because of new address from DHCP) but the ranges overlap (10.0.0.0/24), kernel rejects the new set with EEXISTS. I don't know if this would happen in real life. Does `networkd` always drop the old address (`address_drop()`) before adding the new address (`address_update()`)? If not, the old addresses could be simply dropped from the set before adding new addresses.

Now there's an assumption with directive processing that only one set will ever will be used, but this should be relaxed. The admin could want to use multiple sets in different protocol tables (ARP/bridge/inet/ip/ip6/netdev).

@yuwata @poettering  While working on this, I noticed that `sd_nfnl_socket_open()`, called by `fw_nftables_init()`, eventually calls `socket_open()`, which uses `SOCK_NONBLOCK` flag when opening. issue_context.title: RFE/RFD: lightweight integration of NFT sets for use in firewalls
comments:
Benefit of using NFT sets compared to external daemons is that modifying the set is synchronous but very lightweight operation. For example, `networkd` can set the IP address from DHCP to the set before applying it to the interface, so there are no time windows where the set would be updated too late. This could easily happen if there's an external daemon listening to events (unless PID1 or `networkd` would wait while scripts execute and signal completion).

@poettering @yuwata @keszybz @bluca WDYT?

[libnftnl](https://netfilter.org/projects/libnftnl/index.html) is licensed under GPL2+. Would that be a problem?

Its dependency, [libmnl](https://netfilter.org/projects/libmnl/index.html) is under LGPLv2.1+.
Yes, GPL2 library would be a problem, as the combined work after linking would be GPL2 as a whole - weird license choice for a library?

> Yes, GPL2 library would be a problem, as the combined work after linking would be GPL2 as a whole - weird license choice for a library?

Yes, not very inviting. Luckily our own `sd-netlink` already can process some [netlink messages]( https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/9fa31df62dd504e8f3e43710df504a467ed430fa/src/libsystemd/sd-netlink/netlink-message-nfnl.c).
Conceptually the networkd ip address thing, and the cgroup id thing make sense to me. Not sure I am convinced by the resolved thing, it sucks for access control...

So we recently discussed whether we should add support to .network files to automatically load nft rules files on interface activation. i.e. that if networkd actviates foobar.network we also load the foobar.nft firewall. 

It appears to me that the concept suggested here of maintaining NFT set objects is a more flexible approach, right?

i.e. what model is preferable: having a static firewall ruleset with dynamic sets – or having a dynamic firewall ruleset? It appears to me the former makes more sense.

Thoughts?

I think the models are complementary. Loading rules on interface activation is useful for `netdev` rules, which can't use a set for the interface name. In other cases, set objects may contain information which can be used with static (but also per-interface) rules.

The per-interface rules can be implemented with no changes. Example:

```
# /etc/udev/rules.d/90-netfilter.rules 
SUBSYSTEM!="net", GOTO="netfilter_end"
ENV{SYSTEMD_WANTS}+="nftables-dev@$name.service"
LABEL="netfilter_end"
```

```
# /etc/systemd/system/nftables-dev@.service
[Unit]
Description=nftables for device %i
Documentation=man:nft(8) http://wiki.nftables.org
Wants=network-pre.target nftables.service
Before=network-pre.target shutdown.target
Conflicts=shutdown.target
DefaultDependencies=no
After=nftables.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
RemainAfterExit=yes
StandardInput=null
ProtectSystem=full
ProtectHome=true
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/nft -f /etc/nftables-%i.conf
ExecReload=/usr/sbin/nft -f /etc/nftables-%i.conf

[Install]
WantedBy=sysinit.target
```

```
# /etc/nftables-lan.conf 
#!/usr/sbin/nft -f

table netdev filter {
        chain lan_ingress {
                type filter hook ingress device lan priority filter; policy drop;
        }
}

flush chain netdev filter lan_ingress

table netdev filter {
        chain lan_ingress {
                type filter hook ingress device lan priority filter; policy drop;

                meta protocol vmap {
                     ip : jump validate_ipv4,
                     ip6 : jump validate_ipv6,
                     arp : jump validate_arp
                }
                counter log prefix "[netdev-lan-ingress] " flags all drop
        }
}
```
This uses static device name 'lan', but I suppose I could use `@@DEVICE@@` insted and use `sed` to replace the interface name with `%i` and feed its output in a pipe to `nft`.

Some rules above (like `validate_ipv4`) are defined in static part.

**re: resolved and DNS query nft sets**
I think just that is a great idea, I'm using dnsmasq **v2.87** for this specific use case (easily backported to Debian bullseye).

As you might know [`dnsmasq v2.87`](https://thekelleys.org.uk/gitweb/?p=dnsmasq.git) added the `--nftset` domain name option.
It's great because the nft sets are populated when, and only when, an actual DNS query is performed by the application / service with the ip addresses returned to them by the DNS reply.  It's very efficient.

I had been trying to work out an allowlist firewall using systemd cgroupv2...
Instead I settled on forcing every service and application to use specific Linux users and or groups (one for _every_ that requires any network resources).
nftables is indeed easier, more powerful and flexible, and now better for [statistics](https://github.com/sta-c0000/galaf#generating-statistics).
I've detailed how I'm using nftables with dnsmasq nft sets (with some caveats) here: [Group Allow-List Application Firewall](https://github.com/sta-c0000/galaf)

> **re: resolved and DNS query nft sets** I think just that is a great idea, I'm using dnsmasq **v2.87** for this specific use case (easily backported to Debian bullseye).
> 
> As you might know [`dnsmasq v2.87`](https://thekelleys.org.uk/gitweb/?p=dnsmasq.git) added the `--nftset` domain name option. It's great because the nft sets are populated when, and only when, an actual DNS query is performed by the application / service with the ip addresses returned to them by the DNS reply. It's very efficient.

Thanks, I didn't know about this feature. I have a pretty much complete PR for DNS access control for resolved in #17126. My plan is to integrate it with NFT sets. The advantage of using resolved instead of dnsmasq is tighter integration with NSS (nss_resolve). It uses Unix sockets instead of UDP, so much more information on the calling process is available, which could then be used for filtering.

> I had been trying to work out an allowlist firewall using systemd cgroupv2... 

I think the problem is that the kernel interface for accessing cgroups from NFT filters is poor. The cgroupv1 IDs or cgroupv2 paths should not need to be resolvable when the firewall is installed. Perhaps the kernel should perform path checks at cgroup creation time and then automatically resolve cgroup IDs for NFT. Doing this in userspace is a poor choice. It could work for systemd because it's the entity creating the cgroups in most cases, but I don't think this scales to unprivileged `systemd --user`, containers or delegated cgroups etc.

> Instead I settled on forcing every service and application to use specific Linux users and or groups (one for _every_ that requires any network resources). nftables is indeed easier, more powerful and flexible, and now better for [statistics](https://github.com/sta-c0000/galaf#generating-statistics). I've detailed how I'm using nftables with dnsmasq nft sets (with some caveats) here: [Group Allow-List Application Firewall](https://github.com/sta-c0000/galaf)

What a coincidence, I also discovered GALAF a few days ago. Using a different UID/GID for every application is a nice idea. For system services, this is pretty easy since many services already run with either a fixed UID with `User=` or use `DynamicUser=` and then `meta skuid` can be used for access control. Perhaps the remaining UID 0 services could be convinced to use a different GID (and drop CAP_SETGID). For unprivileged user apps there should be a way to switch to UID/GID per app with [Firejail](https://github.com/netblue30/firejail) or [bubblewrap](https://github.com/containers/bubblewrap) so that it's integrated with other sandboxing features. It would be awesome if also GUI tools like gnome-system-monitor could show network statistics at app level, perhaps even drilling down to each process/thread.

SELinux can be also integrated with firewall tables, but the design choice is that the access rules are on SELinux side. This makes sense, but the actual implementation is a bit weird. It would be simpler if the SELinux domain label for the process or socket could be also used directly on NFT side for further access control.

Further integration idea: `DynamicUser=yes` should be also enhanced so that PID1 would keep a NFT set updated when the dynamic UID is allocated and deallocated. The directive could be for example `DynamicUserNFTSet=nfproto:tablename:setname`. Then the firewall rules for protocol `nfproto` and table `tablename` could use the dynamic UID for access control with `meta skuid != @setname counter drop`.

Another simple integration feature idea for networkd, this time not with firewalls but [NetLabel](https://github.com/netlabel/netlabel_tools) system (SELinux, Smack, perhaps AppArmor and other LSMs too): new directives `Network.IPv4NetLabelUnlabel=` and `Network.IPv6NetLabelUnlabel=` (perhaps the names could be improved...). This would improve handling of dynamic network interfaces with NetLabel subsystem.

Proposed manual page text:

`Network.IPv4NetLabelUnlabel=label...` and `Network.IPv6NetLabelUnlabel=label...`
- These settings provide a method for integrating dynamic network configuration into Linux NetLabel subsystem rules, used by Linux security modules (LSMs) for network access control. The options expect a whitespace separated list of NetLabel labels. The labels must conform to lexical restrictions of LSM labels. When an interface is configured with IP addresses, the addresses and subnetwork masks will be appended to the NetLabel Fallback Peer Labeling rules. They will be removed when the interface is deconfigured. Failures to manage the labels will be ignored.

- As an example for `IPv4NetLabelUnlabel=system_u:object_r:localnet_peer_t:s0` for interface `eth0`, when the interface is configured with an IPv4 address 10.0.0.0/8, networkd performs the equivalent of `netlabelctl` operation `unlbl add interface eth0 address:10.0.0.0/8 label:system_u:object_r:localnet_peer_t:s0` and the reverse when the IPv4 address is deconfigured.

I think this would also help with [NetLabel issue #8](https://github.com/netlabel/netlabel_tools/issues/8), for systems with systemd-networkd. @pcmoore WDYT?

The NetLabel integration seems reasonable to me, although there would likely need to be some additional configuration (or very prominent warnings!) as once you start labeling network traffic a lot of access control points go from dormant to active and it is easy for someone not familiar with the LSM per-packet access controls to get into a bad situation.

I should also add, if NetLabel integration is something systemd is serious about, I can make the netlabel_tools static library a shared library (and likely clean it up a bit too) if systemd wanted to take that approach instead of calling `netlabelctl` directly.

> The NetLabel integration seems reasonable to me, although there would likely need to be some additional configuration (or very prominent warnings!) as once you start labeling network traffic a lot of access control points go from dormant to active and it is easy for someone not familiar with the LSM per-packet access controls to get into a bad situation.

Yes, the static configuration would have to be managed with `netlabelctl` like before, the new directive should be needed only if dynamic interfaces need extra configuration. There should be a warning and maybe a reference to NetLabel docs.

There could be a full-blown implementation, where networkd could be used to configure all NetLabel features, but I don't think that makes too much sense. Testing all features (CIPSO etc) with a CI setup would be also _interesting_ exercise.

> I should also add, if NetLabel integration is something systemd is serious about, I can make the netlabel_tools static library a shared library (and likely clean it up a bit too) if systemd wanted to take that approach instead of calling `netlabelctl` directly.

That would be great, assuming that the license will be compatible with systemd's LGPL2.1. Systemd also has an internal implementation of netlink message handling which could be used.

> > I should also add, if NetLabel integration is something systemd is serious about, I can make the netlabel_tools static library a shared library (and likely clean it up a bit too) if systemd wanted to take that approach instead of calling `netlabelctl` directly.
> 
> That would be great, assuming that the license will be compatible with systemd's LGPL2.1. Systemd also has an internal implementation of netlink message handling which could be used.

It would also need to be dlopen-safe, which usually is not a problem, but worth mentioning. But it looks like it's GPL-2.0-only https://github.com/netlabel/netlabel_tools/blob/main/LICENSE which is a problem - we'd need LGPL-2.1-or-later to use it here

> Testing all features (CIPSO etc) with a CI setup would be also interesting exercise.

We do basic SELinux/NetLabel testing as part of the kernel-secnext automated testing, via the selinux-testsuite, but I wouldn't consider that exhaustive testing.  In some sense, a fully exhaustive test is out-of-scope for the selinux-testsuite.

> That would be great, assuming that the license will be compatible with systemd's LGPL2.1. Systemd also has an internal implementation of netlink message handling which could be used.

... and ...

> ... it looks like it's GPL-2.0-only which is a problem ...

Part of that comes from the original idea that the only consumers of the netlabel_tools static library were going to be tools included in netlabel_tools.  I'm not sure I want to go through the hassle of re-licensing the package/library at this point, especially since systemd already knows how to talk to the kernel via netlink/attributes; it's likely easier and quicker to just have systemd issue whatever NetLabel commands it wants direclty via netlink.

> Part of that comes from the original idea that the only consumers of the netlabel_tools static library were going to be tools included in netlabel_tools. I'm not sure I want to go through the hassle of re-licensing the package/library at this point, especially since systemd already knows how to talk to the kernel via netlink/attributes; it's likely easier and quicker to just have systemd issue whatever NetLabel commands it wants direclty via netlink.

Agreed. The [unlabeled](https://github.com/netlabel/netlabel_tools/blob/d41600dd298a9f8a1621a48e41cc978a557221ac/libnetlabel/mod_unlabeled.c#L362) protocol seems simple (command, iface, secctx, addr+mask), so we can implement it without any new libraries.
Made a separate PR #23269 for NetLabel, since it doesn't use NFT sets.
